name: The Jujube of the Botanic Garden
species: Common Jujube (Ziziphus jujuba, registry recorded as Ziziphus zizyphus, a synonym)

location.address: Near the intersection of Old Garden Road and Rock Springs Road, Fort Worth Botanic Garden, 3220 Botanic Garden Blvd, Fort Worth, TX
location.neighbourhood: Fort Worth Botanic Garden (Rock Springs section), Cultural District

verified_sources: Texas Big Tree Registry (TAMU Forest Service), TreeID 436, lead source only
access: Paid entry. Fort Worth Botanic Garden charges general admission (adults $14, ages 3-15 $8, as of the fee restructure that folded the former separate Japanese Garden charge into one ticket). Open during garden hours.
transport: Inside the Fort Worth Botanic Garden grounds, Cultural District, about 4.5 km west of downtown Fort Worth; no direct rail, nearest Trinity Metro bus routes serve the Cultural District.
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree this is a real, specific tree: (1) Texas Big Tree Registry TreeID 436, coordinates 32.73636/-97.36494, girth 190cm, registry condition rated 2 (of presumably a 1-5 or similar scale), measured May 2020 -- lead source only per licence, not used alone. (2) texastreetrails.org's 'Fort Worth Botanic Garden Champion Tree Trail' page, an independent regional tree-recording project, lists a Jujube stop at 32.73650N/-97.36470W, 'only about 15 feet off the road' at the Old Garden Road / Rock Springs Road intersection -- about 25m from the registry coordinate, close enough to be the same individual tree given GPS precision at that scale. That page states it is the largest jujube tree recorded in the state (45 feet tall) and calls it a DFW Regional Champion. FLAGGED because neither source is freshly dated: the registry measurement is from May 2020 and the trail page carries no visible publish/update date (old FrontPage-era HTML, likely years old). No source reports the tree removed or dead, and the garden's own champion tree trail appears to still be an active, promoted feature (referenced in current garden tour material), which is circumstantial evidence of continued presence rather than proof. A run with time to spare should look for a 2024-2026 dated photo or garden blog post naming this tree specifically. Age not documented anywhere; jujube can live centuries in cultivation but I have no growth-rate basis for this specimen so age_estimate is left empty rather than guessed. Species note: registry uses the older synonym Ziziphus zizyphus; Ziziphus jujuba is the accepted name, recorded per hard rule 9 (canonical name).

name: The Ward Parkway Texas Red Oak

location.address: 2026-2212 Ward Parkway, Fort Worth, TX 76110 (city-owned park land along the parkway)
location.neighbourhood: Park Hill, near TCU and Colonial Country Club

verified_sources: Texas Big Tree Registry (TAMU Forest Service), TreeID 843, lead source only
access: Free. On city-owned park land along Ward Parkway; texastreetrails.org states plainly 'the public can visit the trees within park operating hours.'
transport: In south Fort Worth near TCU, about 5 km south of downtown; no rail stop nearby, reachable by Trinity Metro bus or a short drive/rideshare.
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree: (1) Texas Big Tree Registry TreeID 843, coordinates 32.7175/-97.34972, girth 622cm (very large for the species, ~1.98m diameter), registry condition rated 2, measured July 2026 -- lead source only per licence. (2) texastreetrails.org's DFW National Champion Tree Trail names stop 2 as a Texas Red Oak at 2026-2212 Ward Pkwy, Fort Worth TX 76110, coordinates 32.717166/-97.349816 (within about 40m of the registry point), registered as both a Texas State Champion and, per that page's framing, a National Champion. The same page states explicitly this is 'city owned park land' and 'the public can visit the trees within park operating hours,' which clears the access bar. I could not identify a specific named park for this stretch of parkland via OSM or search (it reads as city right-of-way/parkland rather than a named city park), so the location field describes it as city-owned parkland along Ward Parkway rather than inventing a park name. FLAGGED for recency: the registry measurement (July 2026) is very recent and is itself strong evidence of life, but I found no separately dated 2025-2026 photo or article confirming the tree beyond the registry entry itself, and the trail page carries no visible publish date. No source suggests it has been removed. Age not documented; a Texas red oak this size (622cm girth) would very plausibly be over a century old given typical growth rates for the species on decent soil, but I have no specific published growth-rate figure to derive a band from, so age_estimate is left empty rather than guessed.

name: The Will Rogers Mesquite

location.address: Will Rogers Road South, Will Rogers Memorial Center grounds, Fort Worth, TX 76107
location.neighbourhood: Will Rogers Memorial Center, Cultural District

verified_sources: Texas Big Tree Registry (TAMU Forest Service), TreeID 781, lead source only
https://www.texastreetrails.org/tours/natchamp_trail.html (DFW National Champion Tree Trail, Tree ID 128, National Champion Mesquite)
access: Free. City-owned park land at the Will Rogers Memorial Center; texastreetrails.org states it 'can be visited within park operating hours.'
transport: In the Cultural District, about 4.5 km west of downtown Fort Worth, near the Fort Worth Botanic Garden and museums; reachable by Trinity Metro bus.
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree, and coordinates match almost exactly (within about 15m): (1) Texas Big Tree Registry TreeID 781, girth 478cm (a very large mesquite; typical mature mesquites run under 200cm), condition rated 3, measured June 2024 -- lead source only per licence, second source required. (2) texastreetrails.org's DFW National Champion Tree Trail lists 'National Champion Mesquite,' Tree ID 128, at Will Rogers Rd S, coordinates 32.746899/-97.366116, explicitly noting it stands on 'city owned park land' and 'can be visited within park operating hours.' A general search independently surfaced this same tree described as Fort Worth's National Champion mesquite, called the 'World's Biggest' in popular framing, at the Will Rogers Complex. FLAGGED for two reasons: (a) I could not independently confirm the National Champion status is still current with American Forests' National Register (that register updates periodically and champions can be dethroned); this record is presented as a large, registry-documented, publicly sited mesquite rather than resting on the champion claim. (b) The registry's own measurement (June 2024) is reasonably recent and is itself decent evidence of life, but I found no separate 2025-2026 photo or article. Age not documented; mesquites are slow growing and long lived but I have no species-specific growth-rate figure I trust enough to derive a band, so age_estimate is left empty. Note the Will Rogers Complex hosts large public events (stock shows, etc.) and access during those could be restricted or ticketed; the honest access line covers ordinary park-operating-hours access.

name: The Pioneers Rest Texas Ash

location.address: Pioneers Rest Cemetery, 620 Samuels Avenue, Fort Worth, TX 76102
location.neighbourhood: Near Sundance Square / downtown Fort Worth

verified_sources: Texas Big Tree Registry (TAMU Forest Service), TreeID 19, lead source only
access: Free. Public historic cemetery (National Register of Historic Places, 2021), 620 Samuels Avenue. The main gate is sometimes locked but a public entrance exists on the south end of the west fence; visiting in daylight is recommended. Maintained by the Pioneers Rest Cemetery Association with city involvement.
transport: About 1.2 km northeast of downtown Fort Worth, near Sundance Square, walkable from the city centre.
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree on a regional-champion Texas Ash at this cemetery: (1) Texas Big Tree Registry TreeID 19, girth 213cm (about 68cm / 26.7in diameter), condition rated 3, measured December 2025 -- lead source only per licence. (2) An Arborjet (tree-care company) blog post from June 2019, 'Saving America's Iconic Trees: Pioneers Rest Cemetery in Ft. Worth, Texas,' describes 'the regional champion Texas Ash tree,' diameter 26 inches, at this same cemetery, and reports the City of Fort Worth was having it professionally injected against Emerald Ash Borer with a commitment to keep monitoring and retreating it every 2-3 years at no cost to the city. The 26in diameter reported in 2019 matches closely with the registry's 213cm girth (about 26.7in diameter) measured six years later, consistent growth rather than a different tree. 'ALIVE NOW' evidence is unusually good here: the registry's own measurement date (December 2025, nine months ago) means someone physically re-measured this exact tree very recently, and the 2019 article shows the city was actively investing in keeping it alive against a specific pest threat, which is a stronger signal than a passive listing. Still flagged because I have no post-2019 confirmation that the city continued the EAB treatment programme as promised, only the registry's recent re-measurement, which implies but does not directly state ongoing health. Age not documented; no growth-rate figure I trust for Fraxinus texensis to hand, so age_estimate is left empty rather than guessed. Cemetery access note: it is a public historic cemetery but visitors should use the correct gate; this is an honest caveat rather than a blocker.
